name: Cheonbuin
powers: Marks the royal mandate of the founder king
description: The cheonbuin, the heavenly seal, is the seal that the Samguk Yusa says Hwanung, son of the sky god Hwanin, carried when he descended to Mount Taebaek with three seals to govern the world. In the Dangun foundation myth Hwanung established a sacred city at the summit, legislated for the people, and accepted the prayers of a bear and a tiger who wished to become human; the bear that endured the ordeal of a hundred days in a cave became the woman Ungnyeo, whose son Dangun founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon. The seal is given to the king's descendants as the mark of royal mandate, anchoring Korean sovereignty in the descent of the royal line from heaven. The story is recorded in the Samguk Yusa and the Jewang Ungi, and it is the foundational myth of Korean identity, celebrated in the founding day festival of Gaecheonjeol. The cheonbuin is often paired in royal regalia with the sword of office, and the image of Hwanung descending with the seal is a fixed scene in Korean national symbolism.

name: Geobukseon
powers: Iron-roofed warship that shed fire and boarding parties
description: The geobukseon, the turtle ship, is the armoured warship that Admiral Yi Sun-sin built for the Korean fleet in the 1590s to repel the Japanese invasions of the Imjin War, and it is the most celebrated naval vessel in Korean history. The ship was roofed with an iron-studded shell that shed fire arrows and repelled boarding parties, and it was fitted with cannon that could be fired from the sides while the deck stayed protected. Although the turtle ship was a real and effective warship, it passed quickly into folklore as an invincible protector of the coast, celebrated in songs, tales, and the war memoirs of Admiral Yi himself. Modern scholarship notes that the historical vessels were smaller and less dramatic than later depictions, but the legend endures, and the turtle ship is a national symbol of defence and ingenuity. Reconstructions are displayed and sailed at memorials such as the Hyeonchungsa shrine and the war museum in Seoul, and the turtle ship remains the emblem of Korean naval power.

name: Gogok
powers: Symbol of rank, fertility, and the sun
description: The gogok is the comma-shaped jade ornament threaded onto the gold crowns, belts, and necklaces of the ancient Silla kingdom, excavated in large numbers from the tombs of Gyeongju, and it is the most distinctive form of Korean prehistoric jade. Carved from hard nephrite and often pale green or white, the beads may derive from the shamanic curved beads of the north and are linked by scholars to fertility symbolism and to the bear-woman Ungnyeo's offering in the Dangun foundation myth. In the tombs of Silla's elite the gogok hangs from the crowns and diadems in cascading rows, and the form persisted into the Gaya and Baekje kingdoms. Modern Korean scholarship sees in the curved bead an image of a claw or a moon-crescent, and the gogok appears on the national emblem of the modern Gyeongju region. It remains the emblem of ancient Korean royal regalia and one of the most recognizable objects of the country's archaeological heritage.

name: Bangmangi
powers: Grants whatever the wielder wishes when struck
description: The bangmangi is the magic club of the dokkaebi, the mischievous goblin of Korean folklore, which grants whatever a person wishes when it is struck. In the folktales the dokkaebi owns the club and uses it to summon food, gold, and servants, and clever humans trick the gullible goblin into surrendering it: a thief or a poor man persuades the dokkaebi that a beating with the club will bring a blessing, then runs off with the prize. In other variants the club is swapped, or its possessor uses it to draw endless rice and healing, and the object is so tied to its owner that the dokkaebi and its bangmangi are nearly interchangeable in stories. The club appears in the collected Korean tales of Im Bang and Yi Ryuk and in the oral tradition of the pansori storytellers, and it remains a beloved fixture of Korean children's literature and animation. The bangmangi embodies the dokkaebi's double nature as both threat and source of luck.

name: Yeouiju
powers: Grants wishes; lets the imugi become a dragon
description: The yeouiju is the wish-granting jewel of Korean lore, the glowing orb that a serpent, imugi, must grasp to climb into full dragonhood, and that grants any wish to its holder. In the tales the imugi, a hornless dragon, waits for the jewel to fall from the sky or to be revealed by a righteous person, and the story of the imugi that lost the jewel at the waterfall is among the most famous Korean dragon tales. The yeouiju is also described as the possession of the dragon kings of the sea and of the mountain spirits, and its power is sometimes linked to the moon, whose light it is said to drink. In Buddhist-influenced versions the jewel is identified with the cintamani, the wish-fulfilling gem, and in shamanic tradition it is a shaman's treasure. The yeouiju appears in the imagery of the dokkaebi goblin as well, and it remains one of the most evocative objects of Korean mythic symbolism, standing for the attainment of the unattainable.
